web.title: Adaptive Conformal Inference for Multi-Step Ahead Time-Series Forecasting Online
web.description:
Conformal prediction (CP), described in detail in Shafer and Vovk ([2008](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib7)) and Vovk et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib12)), is a general method for distribution-free uncertainty quantification, using past experience to determine precise levels of confidence in a new prediction. It can be applied to essentially any machine learning method, and has guaranteed properties of validity, provided that the data is drawn from a probability distribution that is exchangeable (see Vovk et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib12)), Section 2.1.1 for details), meaning essentially that any permutation is equally probable. In the online setting, where Reality presents us with successive examples $z_{t}:=(x_{t},y_{t})\in Z:=X\times Y$, each one consisting of an object $x_{t}\in X$ and its associated label $y_{t}\in Y$, CP produces prediction sets, $\Gamma_{t}^{\varepsilon}$ (typically intervals), at a user specified significance level $\varepsilon$, using $z_{1},\dots,z_{t-1}$ and $x_{t}$ as input. They are valid in the sense that the true label, $y_{t}$, is contained in the prediction set with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$, and the error events are independent.^1^^1^1“at

Adaptive conformal inference (ACI), introduced in Gibbs and Candes ([2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib4)), is a method designed to achieve a desired coverage frequency $1-\varepsilon$ even in cases when the data is not exchangeable. Because ACI does not require data to be exchangeable, it has been suggested as a good candidate for producing prediction intervals in time-series forecasting (Zaffran et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib15)). It achieves, at least asymptotically, a user specified target error rate $\varepsilon$, by using a simple online update of the significance level
$$\varepsilon_{t+1}=\varepsilon_{t}+\gamma(\varepsilon-\text{err}_{t}^{%
\varepsilon})$$
where
$$\text{err}_{t}^{\varepsilon}=\begin{cases}1&\text{if $y_{t}\notin\Gamma_{t}^{%
\varepsilon_{t}}$}\\
0&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$

In time-series forecasting, we are often interested in predicting more than just one step ahead, which is known as multi-step ahead forecasting. In this situation, we can not use ACI directly because the online update requires knowledge of the errors immediately, but if we predict $h$ steps ahead, we only learn whether our prediction was correct after $h$ time steps have passed.
The main contribution of this paper is to adapt the ACI algorithm to multi-step ahead forecasts in the online setting. To the best of my knowledge, this has not been done before. ACI has been suggested as part of the adaptive ensemble batch multi-input multi-output conformalised quantile regression (AEnbMIMOCQR) in Sousa et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib8)) which uses bootstrapping, similar to the ensemble batch prediction intervals (EnbPI) algorithm introduced by Xu and Xie ([2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib14)). Another approach to conformal multi-step ahead forecasting, taken in Schlembach et al. ([2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib6)), uses the weighted quantiles method of Barber et al. ([2023](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib2)) together with an inductive conformal predictor in the offline mode.

Empirical studies (Taieb et al., [2012](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib10); Xiong et al., [2013](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib13)) have shown that MIMO strategies tend to outperform recursive strategies that use one-step ahead forecasts to produce the next forecast, which tends to accumulate prediction errors. This is however not an absolute rule, and there are situations where recursive strategies may be a better option.
### 2.1 MIMO conformalised ridge regression
We adapt the conformalised ridge regression (CRR) algorithm (Algorithm 2.4 Vovk et al., [2022](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib12)) to handle multi-step ahead predictions, resulting in the MIMO-CRR algorithm, which is described in alg:mimo-crr.

The ACI algorithm was introduced in Gibbs and Candes ([2021](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib4)). It works in the online setting by a simple update of the significance level. Here we adapt it to handle multi-step ahead forecasts, allowing for different confidence levels and learning rate at different prediction steps.

The Conformal PID control method, introduced in Angelopoulos et al. ([2024](https://arxiv.org/html/2409.14792v1#bib.bib1)), may be viewed as a generalisation of ACI, where ACI is the special case of using only the P part of their method. Future work could investigate the utility of adapting conformal PID to the multi-step ahead forecast setting.

web.title: Adaptive Conformal Inference for Multi-Step Ahead Time-Series Forecasting Online
web.description:
# Adaptive Conformal Inference for Multi-Step Ahead Time-Series Forecasting Online
Jönköping University
JH
Johan Hallberg Szabadváry
## Abstract
The aim of this paper is to propose an adaptation of the well known adaptive conformal inference (ACI) algorithm to achieve finite-sample coverage guarantees in multi-step ahead time-series forecasting in the online setting. ACI dynamically adjusts significance levels, and comes with finite-sample guarantees on coverage, even for non-exchangeable data. Our multi-step ahead ACI procedure inherits these guarantees at each prediction step, as well as for the overall error rate. The multi-step ahead ACI algorithm can be used with different target error and learning rates at different prediction steps, which is illustrated in our numerical examples, where we employ a version of the confromalised ridge regression algorithm, adapted to multi-input multi-output forecasting. The examples serve to show how the method works in practice, illustrating the effect of variable target error and learning rates for different prediction steps, which suggests that a balance may be struck between efficiency (interval width) and coverage.t

A significant limitation of standard Conformal Prediction is its reliance on the assumption of exchangeability—essentially, that the order of the data does not affect its joint probability distribution. Time-series data inherently violates this assumption due to temporal dependencies, trends, and non-stationarity. To address this, Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI) was developed to adjust the significance level of the predictor dynamically based on past performance. However, ACI was originally designed for one-step-ahead forecasting where the error is observed immediately. This paper adapts ACI for the multi-step-ahead setting, providing a method to maintain coverage guarantees even when the feedback for a prediction is delayed by several time steps.

The paper proposes a vectorized extension of ACI to manage multiple forecast horizons simultaneously. Instead of maintaining a single target error rate and learning rate, the method utilizes vectors for both. Let be the vector of desired miss-coverage rates and be the vector of learning rates for each horizon.
The adaptive update rule for the significance levels at time is defined as:
In this equation, represents element-wise multiplication. The key to making this work in an online multi-step environment is the construction of the error vector . At any time , we observe the true value . This single observation allows us to evaluate the accuracy of several previous predictions: the 1-step-ahead prediction made at , the 2-step-ahead prediction made at , and so on, up to the -step-ahead prediction made at . The error vector is thus defined as:
where is a binary indicator (0 or 1) signifying whether the true value fell outside the prediction interval generated steps ago. This mechanism ensures that every prediction horizon is updated as soon as its corresponding ground truth becomes available, allowing the system to remain as responsive as possible.
## Base Predictor: MIMO Conformalized Ridge Regression
To demonstrate the adaptive framework, the paper employs a Multi-Input Multi-Output (MIMO) strategy combined with Conformalized Ridge Regression (CRR). In the MIMO approach, a single model is trained to map a window of past observations (lags) directly to a vector of future values. This differs from recursive strategies where a 1-step model is applied repeatedly, which can lead to error accumulation.
The MIMO-CRR algorithm calculates "conformity scores" (essentially residuals) for each step in the horizon. It uses these scores to construct prediction intervals that satisfy the significance levels determined by the adaptive update rule. For computational efficiency in an online setting, the ridge regression parameters are updated using the Sherman-Morrison formula, which allows for the recursive update of matrix inverses without recomputing them from scratch at every time step.

[Adaptive conformal predictions for time series](https://alphaxiv.org/abs/2202.07282)
This paper is highly relevant as it is cited for specifically proposing ACI as a strong candidate for time-series prediction. This establishes the direct motivation for the current work, which builds upon that suggestion to create a practical multi-step ahead forecasting method.
